74.ch: Trent's band: Texas, St. Louis and the road east

74.t: Mouse Randolph, Swazey and the pay on the St. Louis boats
74.s: Randolph replaces Swazey; why he left for Terry; Trent clears $70 against others' $35, though no white hotels open to them.
74.ch: Trent's band: Texas, St. Louis and the road east

74.t: The Savoy week and what it paid (second version)
74.s: A week at the Savoy, uncertain competing bands, and the low pay of fifty dollars a week.
74.ch: Trent's band: Texas, St. Louis and the road east
74.q: That's right. It wasn't Fess because we had seen Fess in Chicago when we were there on vacation, but we didn't play Chicago, but Fess was still in Chicago when we played there, but it wasn't against Fess. I don't remember who it was.

74.t: WFAA broadcasts, dance tours and a year and a half at the hotel
74.s: The band broadcasts on a powerful station, books its own dances at $75-90 a man, and stays a year and a half.
74.ch: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
74.q: We were broadcasting, one of the first bands to broadcast over this powerful station WFAA. It was a good thousand watt station years ago. They got us all the way up to Canada and it was a powerful station. That's the reason when Trent's band went on a tour, we would make from 75 to 80 or 90 dollars…

473.t: The Vendome in Buffalo: tips, entertainers and playing in odd keys
473.s: Luke Stewart held a steady four-piece job at the Vendome for $35 a week, with the dancer sharing tips and customers requesting songs in difficult keys.
473.ch: Midwest bands: Hardy Brothers, Helvey and Buffalo

So we got back, we got back to see them all and they was doing pretty good. Luke was at the -- had a regular job now, a steady job, in the Vendome, you know. He…

473.s: A year later Jones explained he earned $125 with Stuff and so never answered the letter; Dorsey gave him $100 and Dance remarks that Benny Goodman was tight with money too.
473.q: But I was getting a hundred and twenty-five with him. So, well, these are the little things that went on. You know. But now -- so I never even answered the letter. I didn't even bother about answering the letter. So now we leave California. My wife is with me. The second time I was out there. So we…

473.t: Eleven years with Cab: weekly salary from $110 to $250
473.s: Cab paid about $90 when others paid $70; Jones began at $110 in 1941, reached $125, and was on $250 in 1952, working every week, with Hilton Jefferson there throughout.
473.ch: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
473.q: Oh, he was with him when I joined and he was with him when I left, so he had to be with him over 11 years. I was there 11 years. Never had no idea I would stay that long. No idea in the world. And Fletcher had sent me this letter too. "If you ever get tired of where you're at, come on back here."…

473.t: Sidemen who learn their worth demand more money: Johnny Hodges, Clyde Lucas
473.s: Stanley Dance and Jones discuss how soloists learn what others earn and ask for raises, citing a current drummer who wanted Cozy's pay and Basie's indifference to drummer Clyde Lucas.
473.ch: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
473.q: wakes up. Just like the drummer we're having trouble with now, see. I think one of them must have told him, "Cozy was getting this. Cozy was getting so and so." Because Sammy said, I don't have anything to do with it. So the guy's a good drummer, beautiful, you know, and what he did, he said,…

473.t: Poor pay and unfulfilled share-and-share-alike promises in Lunceford's band
473.s: College dates paid $10 a night with gas and truck costs deducted; Lunceford promised shares but arrangers like Willie Smith and Wilcox got nothing extra, and Jones left before finding out.
473.ch: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
473.q: And then he made it even still better, because I had to quit. I had to quit after -- I didn't stay a year. Well, we was quitting all the time anyhow, going to different things. And I liked being with them because I liked the way they played, but they didn't work all the time. Sometimes you got…

473.t: Filling in for Bunny Berigan with Tommy Dorsey and the $3,750 offer
473.s: Jonah sat in at Dorsey's Newark gig when Berigan was drunk and was heckled by Chick Webb at the Savoy; later in Los Angeles Dorsey offered a job, sending a ticket but never naming a salary until a letter offered $3,750 a year.
473.q: So we were talking -- I think we were playing in a place in Newark called the Merry-go-Round, with Stuff, and Tommy was getting ready to -- this was way before Charlie, now, you understand, before Charlie Shavers, and so Bunny, he can't make it this night. He gets a little tipsy and he can't make…

69.t: Pay in Harry James's band compared with Duke's
69.s: He earned more with James at first, but Duke paid more when he thought he'd lose him; only Hodges and Carney earned well.
69.ch: Harry James, Bellson and the return to Duke
69.q: Oh, no, I don't think so. Duke always had, like, Johnny Hodges, Harry Carney -- Lawrence, but Lawrence never made as much money as Johnny or Harry Carney made, and I guess that's about all. Maybe a couple other guys -- I don't know how much they made, but that's the only one that really made money…

69.s: Nobody had a written contract with Duke; Tizol insisted on a weekly wage, work or not, with extractions extra.
69.ch: Harry James, Bellson and the return to Duke
69.q: It's only so many ways that he'd pay you off. About to split the one nighters with theatre, with recording and this and the other. That's when I told him, "No, you give me so much a week -- you give me so much every week, work or don't work." But extractions come cost extra.

69.t: Not 'stolen' from James; the Philadelphia concert pay
69.s: Rose says Duke took back Juan, who had left Duke first; Tizol insisted on a full week's pay for the Philadelphia concert.
69.ch: Harry James, Bellson and the return to Duke
69.q: Yeah, I wanted to come to California, because I hadn't been here. I used to come here, like I say before, I used to come here just once a year, you know, for Christmas, and I knew the band was coming this way, so I told Duke, "I was going out for six weeks. For six weeks, I'd be out here in…

He called me when we were living up on in New York -- he called me up once, and I wanted to know what he wanted, while he was playing one of those theatres on Broadway. I went over there and he wanted to offer me $125. I said, "I make more than that…

69.t: Playing the Ziegfeld Follies and the Cotton Club for $125 a week
69.s: He played the Follies from eight, then raced by taxi to the Cotton Club until three, for $125 a week, unsure whether there was a night off.
69.q: So I joined the band, and we used to play in the Zigfield show at night, and after the show, we would get in two taxicabs and run right over to the Cotton Club and play over there -- and we'd play at the Cotton Club until three o'clock. We had two shows, and he gave me $125 a week, which was a lot…

121.t: Ila show for Larry McKinley pays $10
121.s: Ridgley, Earl King and Ernie Cato packed the ILA show; he brought ten pieces for $150 and McKinley gave him $10.
121.q: But I'm saying, that was an experience I had, and that song, in the same old way, went to be a pretty good seller because I remember, uh, Earl King, Ernie Cato, and myself, we were at the, uh, at the ILA, we paid on the show for Larry McKenna. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And I, uh, what Earl King had, trick…

121.t: Playing the Dew Drop and nightly pay
121.s: Two years at the Dew Drop around 1954-56 for about $15 a night, and union scale.
121.q: Yeah. See, at the Dew Drop, that's another thing. See, I played at the Dew Drop at one stretch, and I'll say I've been trying to remember, it had to be before I went to Milano, and I think around 1954. I played there almost two years straight. And I think so, because when I left the Dew Drop, I…

121.t: First hundred-dollar night with Big Curtis
121.s: Christmas night in Opelousas on the road with Big Curtis, who underpaid the band until Ridgley spoke up.
121.q: First time. We were, and this was in 1953. 52? Or 53. And I was with Big Curtis. He came, got me, we're going on the road. He went to Nashville. But Christmas night, we played in Opelousa. Packed up like this. I don't know what it was. I can't remember, but I do know this. When we knocked off that…

121.t: Cosimo's studio sound, then the ILA dance with Earl King and Cato
121.s: Ridgley, Earl King and Cato had hot records, played the ILA hall for McKinley, and he charged $150 for ten pieces.
121.q: Cosmos would luck up and get one, you know, and then he'd miss, and then he'd luck up and get another. But when he was on Dumaine Street, see that was when we all, everything sounded like it was in a little box, although the fat man came out of there. And Jewel King, three times seven, and a lot of…

137.t: Circus pay of about $25 a week
137.s: The 101 Ranch paid around $25 a week with room and board, good money; others earned $40-50 and he saved in the bank.
137.ch: Circus shows and learning to voice
137.q: Yeah, well, the guys was up in the money then, those guys that could read anything. I was getting about $25 a week, room and board and everything.

137.t: Steady salary at Moby Dick's and the social security story
137.s: It was his first straight-salary job: scale plus five percent of the cash registers, and he paid the owner's social security taxes.
137.ch: Long Island years and Battle's estate

137.t: How cooperative bands split the money
137.s: Territory bands were cooperative: Moten rented halls, paid expenses, and divided the take equally, believing sidemen were worth as much as the leader.
137.ch: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
137.q: Well, I tell you how it went with the Benny Morton band. They promote their own dances. He'd rent a big hall like the agents do now. He'd go down and rent a big auditorium. And they'd write themselves. He'd get some men on the door and put out some publicity. And when night come, when they'd divide…

137.t: The Lunceford style and teaching six-part harmony
137.s: Lunceford was a novelty band with dancers, glee club and trio; Durham voiced six-part harmony for a five-horn section and left because pay stopped at $60-65.

166.t: Sacramento after-hours job with the silver-dollar kitty and radio show
166.s: His own four-piece played an after-hours spot, gamblers filled the kitty, and he also did a minstrel-style radio show.

166.q: And we had a kitty sit in front of the bandstand with one of those old graphonola contr welded to a box. And our salary was guaranteed $25 a week. And if the kitty didn't make it, the owner put the rest with it.

That was, I'd say, around '41, and anything that he bought, Oscar Moore had to buy something better. Because Oscar…

166.s: Simmons earned about $300 weekly with uniform and travel pay; Goodman's wife issued checks.

166.q: Well, I was making 125 dollars a week, salary-wise, but then I got paid for wearing the uniform. And I got paid for extra record dates. And I got paid -- we did the Holland Furnace broadcast show, 'Tuesday at Ten,' that was a tune that he recorded, 'Tuesday at Ten.' And actors and actresses

231.s: After the Nazarro split agencies wanted to cut his pay; he recalls the original $100 a week and Nazarro's refusal to pay $125.

231.t: Before Sinatra and Crosby: Buck and Bubbles came first
231.s: He says they played the Paramount before Sinatra, Crosby and Burns and Allen, yet earned little.
231.ch: The 1920s road: dance style and management
231.q: Listen, well before Frank Sinatra, before Bing Crosby, before all these guys, we were before all of them. They've been introduced to us to the extent that they've got to come to where we were. We're not going to where they were because they were

231.t: Pay for Porgy and Bess and Nazarro's handling
231.s: They earned about $750 or $800 a week for two, less than the Follies, and he blames himself rather than race or Nazarro.
231.ch: Porgy and Bess and Varsity Show
231.q: That was it. That's what I'm trying to say to you now. The other one was when Nazarro was trying to get another act in our stead on another job. This way, this guy was trying to undersell Buck and Bubbles for less money than what they should get.

231.t: Underpaid always; Lou Irwin and the Jerome Kern show
231.s: Bubbles grumbled about pay and management; after learning Lou Irwin could have won more for the Kern show he began setting his own salary.
231.ch: Brawls, the Ink Spots and boyhood recollections
231.q: "What did he ever do?" "How long has he been there?" What school did he go to," all that. "He's been on Broadway" so-and-so, so-and-so. That's what did it, you know. So I wasn't displeased about nothing but one thing. I was displeased about the management and displeased about the money received for…

0.t: Leaving Mamie Smith and the salary
0.s: He left in February 1924, stayed in New York, and says they were paid well.
0.ch: Mamie Smith and the New York dance bands
0.q: Oh, I left her there in February, 1924. I stayed with up to '25, and that's, I started staying (unintelligible) in New York, went down and worked in the dance group.

0.t: Pay in 1926 and civil service afterwards

0.ch: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life

120.t: Salary and the make-up of the Meroff band
120.s: He earns $11,500 a year at 22 and spends it on cars, booze and chorus girls; the band has twelve violins, two pianos, tuba and string bass.
120.ch: Benny Meroff and Chicago's jazz scene
120.q: But, can you imagine what $11,500 would be today-- well, anyway, as I said - that's a lot of money because being a guy that never really made any great big money, I didn't know what to do with it. I bought big cars and lots of booze and chased chorus girls.

120.t: Outside weekend jobs and college dates
120.s: Condon let him take Sunday and college dates with a replacement; the band picked up a hundred dollars playing Yale and Connecticut.
120.q: Oh, I went out many times. I'd say - Ed, you mind if I-- I would like to go out. I'd like to get a band; I had lots of offers from booking agents - of course, could you get a group together and I'll send you to Cleveland, Cincinnati - send you around.

120.t: Pay with the Seattle Harmony Kings
120.s: About $80 a week plus extra private parties and recording.
120.ch: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
120.q: Because we were doing some recording and we were playing high class jobs; we had a lot of extra work. We were always doing some extra thing - we always had some little thing going - a private party -- in the afternoon, we'd play some afternoon things. And, such things. He always had us making extra…

120.t: Jazz clubs that paid jazz bands too little
120.s: Societies with thousands of dues-paying members hire the veterans cheaply, paying $100 to him and $35 to sidemen at a packed concert.
120.q: Yes - well, I think they were taking advantage of the fact that our kind of music wasn't making it. But, it really was. It really was with them it was. And, they figured they could get us cheap because we weren't working that much.

237.t: Pay of $2.50 a night and tips at the Spinning Wheel
237.s: Early-thirties Kansas City work paid little; nine to five for $2.50 plus tips, with visits back and forth to Basie at the Reno.
237.q: We would play 9:00 o'clock until 5:00 in the morning off the Spinnin' Wheel (Inaudible). And your highest payment was $2.50 --

237.t: Moten's pay and work in Kansas City
237.s: Moten got the best big-band jobs and paid well, with scale then about $6 a night.
237.ch: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
237.q: Yes. Now, as I can remember it, Benny began to just grab up most of the work in Kansas City, you know, most of the big band work. At this time --

237.s: At 12th and Troost Lovett visited Basie at the nearby Reno on intermissions; his band got $2.50 a night, the leader $3.
237.ch: Kansas City rooms and Piney Brown
237.q: Well, I was working at the Spinning Wheel at 12th and Truce and the Reno Nightclub I guess was about a couple of blocks down on the same side of the street and when we'd have intermission, I would go down and see Basie, talk to him until my time was up, you understand what I mean, and then when…

237.t: Twelve years with Julia Lee at Milton's
237.s: Just the two of them for over 12 years; he recalls the record King Sized Papa and says the kitty paid them more than Milton did.
237.q: Oh, she was wonderful. And we -- Milton didn't have to pay us many times, you know. We had a big kitty there, you know, and we'd make our salary in the kitty. He didn't have to pay us a lot of times.

7.t: Paying the band in odd change and the savings-account idea
7.s: As paymaster at $66.66 a week, Thomas drew exact change and proposed a band savings account, which the men soon quit.

I used to have to go the bank every day...I used to go to the cashier and draw the amount of money I needed to get change. Because the…

7.t: Doubling money: theatre dates and the Big Broadcast earnings
7.s: He imagines what a band bank would have grown to, describes doubling pay and the hourly film scale, and a California tour cancelled.
7.ch: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
7.q: I just went to the bank and got all the money, and gave everybody their money back. But in hindsight, if we had kept that up, when we started making more money we could have put in twenty dollars a week or twenty-five dollars a week, and man, we could have run a bank account up to thousands of…

7.t: What the band earned compared with ordinary jobs
7.s: At $66 a week they earned double the Savoy's pay and triple a laborer's, plus hundred dollars doubling in theatres.
7.q: Right. Yeah, we were making big money. We were making double the money we made at the Savoy. We were doubling the scale at the Savoy. See, they had a way of going downtown, and by playing so long they could get a scale okay. Because the Savoy did it...

7.t: Cotton Club break when Duke went to California; the Savoy deal
7.s: The band took Duke's place, and the Savoy and Moe Gale's concessions paid fifty dollars a week.
7.q: I think it was Three Little Words. We can check it. Anyway, Mills got involved with the band through Moe Gale, who was at the Savoy. See, we kind of like... We belonged to the Savoy. I didn't know the business side of it, but the Savoy took the band over. And we used to make fifty dollars a week…

78.s: The men earned about $75 to $85 a week, equal to $150 in 1975 terms.
78.ch: Connie's Inn, Duke Ellington and the Swingland band
78.q: You know, I think these guys were getting around 75 or either 85 dollars a week. This is what the deal was at that time. And that was a lot of money, though.

78.s: He was salaried rather than paid per chart, about $200 a week, equal to $400 in 1975, and inspiration was better when the leader allowed freedom.
78.ch: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk

78.t: Collegians' pay and jobs around Ohio
78.s: After three years the Collegians had regular jobs; $150 a night in Cleveland, $200 at the Crystal Ballroom in Cincinnati, split equally.
78.ch: Childhood, first teachers and the Wilberforce Collegians
78.q: So we had these Collegians for three years in Wilberforce before we actually got -- I mean could, you know, real good, and we got so they knew us in the State of Ohio. We had regular jobs.

78.t: Arranging for Charlie Barnet: two charts a week at $225
78.s: In 1939-40 in New York Horace was salaried at about $225 a week to write two arrangements weekly for Barnet's 19 pieces, mostly staying home, subbing once for pianist Bill Miller.
78.ch: Arranging for Fletcher, Goodman and Barnet
78.q: I played a short period with him when -- he had a little piano player named Bill Miller. Excellent pianist. He's out in Hollywood now in one of the studios -- arranging and playing. 58.t: Chicago pay with Tiny Parham, Oliver Bibbs and Francois
58.s: He compares salaries, explains how Francois's men kicked back part of their pay, and admits whiskey cost him.
58.q: Yeah, I made good money with Tiny Palm and I made my best money with Oliver Bibbs. So Oliver Bibbs, I made the best money with him. I got ninety, eighty-five dollars, Tiny Palm, but I got a hundred dollars flat every week with this Oliver Bibbs.

58.t: Carnival pay and saving money on the Royal American
58.s: He explains how costs shrank carnival wages, the Royal American bonus, and how he saved money gambling.
58.q: All that's the same, you make good salary but the money would go, you have to let it go for your living expenses, you got laundry and all that stuff, they don't pay for nothing for you, you got to pay for everything. Mm-hmm. For yourself.

58.s: Punch says pay began at two or two and a half dollars a man and reached five dollars when he left.
58.ch: Records, rivals and New Orleans bands
58.q: No, they just paid us maybe two dollars a man or two and a half, something like that. That was the beginning. Then they come up around five dollars a man. When I left the yard, that's what they was giving me, five dollars a man. The leader gets sick. Dollars worth of aspirin? Well it must have been…

104.t: Union scale, six-day weeks and a one-nighter by plane
104.s: Union scale was $550 for a six-day week; a one-day trip by small plane with Safranski and Lamond paid about $350, and Metropole musicians were paid abysmally.
104.ch: New York clubs and the Embers trio
104.q: When we started, I think scale was $550, union scale that was. Then he might have been magnanimous and given us $600. This is also less commission, and it was a six-day week. Yet it didn’t seem to dismay anybody.

104.t: Pay and the club owner at The Hickory House
104.s: Trio salary of about $550-700 and the cheap owner.
104.q: Well when you say a club date, you don’t mean like a club date for like a wedding, that’s what we call club dates, like a wedding.

104.t: Club pay in the early 1950s: scale, commissions and free coffee
104.s: A trio at the Hickory House earned about $550 to $600 a week between three people, minus agent commission and union dues, and the owner John Popkin complained about free coffee.
104.ch: New York clubs and the Embers trio
104.q: Yeah, it was different, but it was awfully low, and I . . . when I think of how little . . . I can only pinpoint the Hickory House. I think it was something like $550 or $600, between three people.

372.t: Overall Kenton verdict, pay, the price of horns and leaving
372.s: He felt part of the band, was in debt on a small salary, discusses horn prices and endorsements, and why he left.
372.q: I think so, yeah. I really felt a part of that band and I couldn’t sit in the back of the bus with them so I never got to really know and hang out with them. Again, this has been the story of a lot my situations that I didn’t get to know people that intimately from my shyness or whatever. I always…

372.t: How Stan Kenton hired him and the Innovations orchestra
372.s: Kenton phoned him personally; Kirchner explains his financial loss on the Innovations band.
372.q: Yes. I was very pleased and surprised. Apparently, Richie Kamuca was joining the band the same day. He said: “I’m trying for more of a jazz band now.”

372.t: The Tristano group's anger when he joined Kenton
372.s: He explains taking Kenton's job to support five kids, and how Tristano and the students treated him as a traitor.
372.ch: The Tristano group and leaving for Kenton
372.q: We pretty much had a couple sets where [we called tunes], I think, then we just played the melodies . . . ballads and stuff.

87.s: Young earned $10 a night on one-nighters, Willie Smith more, and Sy Oliver was paid $5 for arranging and copying "Blue Heaven."
87.q: didn't make so much money. Willie Smith was top man in Lunceford's band, and I don't know what Willie made, but I understand he was getting around $100.00 a week.

87.s: Barnet had family money and paid Young about $50 a week more; he stayed about a year and did not record with him.
87.ch: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
87.q: I guess -- I don't think he was that generous or anything, but he did pay pretty well because he didn't have to keep the lines in for himself. He had money, came from a money family. So he could -- I don't know how it worked, but I know he paid well.

87.t: Pay and show rehearsals at the Grand Terrace
87.s: He earned about $44 a week, at most $68, playing three long shows nightly; shows were rehearsed for weeks.
87.ch: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
87.q: Oh, nothing hardly. Let me see. In the early '30's, I think I made about $44.00 a week. And the most we got in there was I think -- when we worked in the Grand Terrace was about $68.00 a week. That's the most we ever got and we worked from 10 to 4. And we played three long shows a night, about hour…

106.s: Briggs earned about $75 a week as lead trumpet, the lowest musicians $50, and Withers and Bechet roughly $80-100.
106.ch: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
106.q: You're telling me. As far as the band was concerned, the lowest price was about $60.00, a week. $50.00. $60.00 and $50.00. The very lowest for a musician was $50.00.

106.t: Rector's Club and pooling pay for Dad Cook
106.s: Bechet and Peyton doubled with Mitchell's Rector's Club and made good money, while Briggs and others pooled pay to cover Cook's expenses without his knowing.
106.ch: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
106.q: And when we finished at the Palais de Hammersmith, Bechet and Benny Peyton's bunch, they continued and they doubled, then doubled with the Rector's Club which was owned by Mr. Mitchell, they played two jobs.

106.t: Noble Sissle hires him at $300 a week
106.s: Via violinist Andre Roseman, Sissle offered Briggs a post at the Ambassador and Ciro's, paying $300 weekly with responsibility for floor shows; he stresses playing quietly, unlike Guy Lombardo.
106.ch: Paris, the Blackbirds and Noble Sissle
106.q: And I stayed with them three months until Noble Sissle, still through the intermediary of Andro Roseman, who was with us as a violin player, with the Syncopated Orchestra, he was with Noble Sissle's Orchestra at the time, in London, and he wired me, saying Noble would like to contact me for his…

758.t: Zack Whyte in Cincinnati and leaving over money
758.s: He stayed two weeks with Zack Whyte, with Sy Oliver as roommate, and left over leaders pleading poverty; his reputation was that he would not stay.
758.q: : Yeah. I worked with him with McKinney's, you know. Let me see. Now, where did I go from Detroit? From Detroit I went to Cincinnati to join Zack Whyte.

758.t: Wages and cheap suits in the 1930s
758.s: Roy made thirty-two dollars at the Savoy and bought cheap suits, noting how far money went.
758.q: : Well, I made thirty-two dollars in the Savoy, and every two weeks I bought me a suit. It wasn't a hundred-dollar suit. There was a cat that... Woolworth's was the place then. Woolworth's was the thing. I bought all them suits, and all of them went out of style. The suits all had buttons on the…

758.s: Roy blew a week's savings treating friends and notes that he and Ben Webster were the only ones who saved.
758.q: : Yeah. And from the Famous Door, I went with Fletcher. So I took all the little bread I had saved and just (?) me a whole week and blew the whole goddamn thing,

18.s: He made $60 a week while Goodman, as a leader downtown, made about $75.
18.ch: Russell and Armstrong years, Goodman and the road
18.q: Yeah, the leader always gets more.

18.t: Joe Glaser, and pay in Armstrong's band
18.s: He earned more than the usual scale, $15 a night against $10 for trombonist George Washington.
18.ch: Cincinnati, Buffalo, Russell and Fletcher Henderson
18.q: That's exactly right. The trombone player he got $10 and I got $15 and when he gave it to me, he got mad. That was George Washington.

18.t: Earning $200 a week and giving money away
18.s: He made $200 weekly, spent it freely and helped relatives.

99.t: Charles on the band's low pay in 1942
99.s: Charles notes the salary was below par when he went into service as people worked the graveyard shift.
99.q: was really below par when I went in the service. After the people had started working the graveyard shift, AND THE WAR GOING. (unintelligible).

99.t: Did the Plantation pay later bands $4,000 a week?
99.s: Pillars doubts the band pay rumor and says big acts and booking agents got more than local bandleaders.
99.q: If I know the people who owned that place, they didn't pay the band that kind of money. That was the kind of money they paid for the shows. That was the kind of money they paid for the shows, and I'll tell you, I think Noble Sissel got -- in fact, all of them made more money than we made, because…

99.t: What the band earned and the steady grind
99.s: The leaders made only slightly more than the sidemen, never got into big money, and compare their steady local work to bands living on buses.
99.ch: Last years of the band and reflections
99.q: It really was. It was hard, but it was good. Now, the time we was at the Plantation, we didn't make no money to amount to anything. I mean, in this respect. Now, when the band was making $25 a week -- no, when the band was making $22 a week, we were making $30 a week. When the band went up to $25 a…

412.t: Pay in the early New York years: $7 dates and $25 a night
412.s: Hodes hired Condon and others for $7 on a City College date. He says Nick's paid no more than $40 a week and that Ryan's and Condon's still pay little.
412.ch: Jam sessions, pay and the Vanguard (retyped)
412.q: : That he could do it. Very few can do it today, in my opinion, again. But anyway, I'm finally at Rind's and I'm finally invited to play, one Sunday afternoon. It wasn't a big deal. I think I paid either seven or ten dollars. I remember playing City College and I hired Eddie Condon, Mezz Crow,…

412.t: Pay in the early New York years: $7 dates and $25 a night
412.s: Hodes hired Condon and others for $7 on a City College date. He says Nick's paid no more than $40 a week and that Ryan's and Condon's still pay little.
412.ch: Jam sessions, pay and the Vanguard (corrected typing)
412.q: That he could do it. Very few can do it today, in my opinion, again. But anyway, I'm finally at Rind's and I'm finally invited to play, one Sunday afternoon. It wasn't a big deal. I think I paid either seven or ten dollars. I remember playing City College and I hired Eddie Conlon, Mezzrow, Cliff…

412.t: Change-the-band bosses and a Class Z scale night
412.s: Hodes tells stories about bosses who change the band when business is down. He tells one boss to tear up his name after a night's pay of $17.15.
412.q: And this is the thinking, the typical thinking of bosses. Another story was working the Sahara. And the boss is sitting at the bar with a girl. And I heard that story.

235.t: Paying sidemen fifteen dollars and the Tennessee Waltz tip
235.s: He paid sidemen about fifteen dollars a night, and a woman once tipped twenty dollars for Tennessee Waltz.
235.ch: The Paradise and life in Queens
235.q: : was playin' piano, somebody--some woman--wanted "Tennessee Waltz" and she had 20 dollars. I says, "Look here man," I says, "You all want to play 'Tennessee Waltz'? Here's 20 dollars." They say, "Yeah, just start the lead and we got you." (laughter) The "Tennessee Waltz", I'll be dawgone. I just…

235.t: Thirty dollars a week with Kelly Martin; Vido Musso and Roy Eldridge
235.s: His Club Congo pay was thirty to forty dollars, spent on room, food, reeds and music; he met Vido Musso and Roy Eldridge in Detroit.
235.q: I think, when I look back, Kelly Martin paid us. Yeah. I think it was thirty or forty dollars, which was good money for me. My God, I thought it was a fortune. Hahahaha.

235.t: Sixty dollars a week in Chicago and the jitney cabs
235.s: His pay for the 33 weeks was about sixty dollars, with an eight-dollar room at the Oakwood Manor Hotel and dime jitney rides.
235.q: think my room was eight dollars a week. And they have these jitney cabs in Chicago. You can ride as long as you want to for a dime as long as you didn't turn the corner. So I lived at the Oakwood Manor Hotel, so we walk up this block and catch this jitney, shoot, for a dime we was home. And those…

95.t: Pay as chorus girl, ballad singer and blues singer
95.s: She earned about $10.50 a week as a chorus girl and $13 as a ballad singer, and says she only learned to sing the blues when records came out.
95.q: Well, if you did a solo, if you were a blues singer, you got good pay. If you was a chorus girl, you got around 10.50 a week and if you did ballads, you got about maybe $12.00 a week.

95.t: Record pay, spending and clothes in the 1920s
95.s: She was paid about a hundred dollars a record, supported her brother and husband's mother, and saved nothing.
95.ch: Friends, New York life and recording routine
95.q: Well, they paid me -- I never did make but one record, I always made a gang of records. And then they would pay you dollars a record, you know. I mean, (unintelligible).

95.t: Why she became a blues singer and her heavy voice
95.s: Blues singers earned more, and she says her voice grew heavy after she got wet, which suited the blues.
95.q: Yeah, told me to get the blues, told me (unintelligible). Otherwise, I never would have because I was a ballad singer, you know.

454.t: Paying sidemen versus Hampton, South American touring and being voodooed
454.s: Mingus paid sidemen over $1,000 a week by the night while Hampton paid by the week; his illness and Katherine Dunham.
454.ch: Ellington, singers, the book and closing
454.q: There's no future in it. To play jazz, you've got to be foolish. You've got to not want money, you got to not want to pay your rent on time. Only guys that can afford jazz now is the white guys. Lionel Hampton, man, he's still paying his men in these days, man, $400 a week. I was paying my drummer…

454.t: Norman Granz, George Wein and what jazz musicians were paid
454.s: Mingus says promoters paid too little, citing his cheap first Jazz at the Philharmonic and Louis Armstrong's guarantee.
454.ch: Kid Ory, Hampton, Ellington and Ben Webster
454.q: (Inaudible), I never worked for him. When Billie Holiday demanded that he hire me because (inaudible), I did the first jazz philharmonic cheap because he's (inaudible). To work for nothing, because these two guys (inaudible) money. With George ______, they never paid enough money, man. Just before…

454.t: Retyped pages: Granz, Wein and Hampton's pay
454.s: Repeated passages on promoters' pay and Hampton's underpayment.
454.q: (Inaudible), I never worked for him. When Billie Holiday demanded that he hire me because (inaudible), I did the first jazz philharmonic cheap because he's (inaudible). To work for nothing, because these two guys (inaudible) money. With George ______, they never paid enough money, man. Just before…

115.t: Cooperative pay in Lloyd Hunter's band
115.s: Hunter's band split receipts after expenses, so $15 a night was good, bookers took theirs first, and some nights paid two dollars.
115.q: No, it wasn't, it really wasn't. Now, with Lloyd Hunter's band, this is what you would call a consolidated band.

115.s: Redd paid a flat $100 a week, which was big money compared with New York scale of the time.
115.q: Well, when I got there, it was more.

115.s: Basie wanted him for a new small band; Gus bargained from $125 to $135, ten dollars above the others.
115.q: And so when he got Butch, well, they came back in town, and I was playing with Cootie's band at the Savoy again. And so he came by the Savoy and told me he wanted to talk to me.

124.t: Gig pay and where club dates were played
124.s: Gigs paid twenty-five to forty dollars a night; they discuss hotels, weddings and New Jersey weekend dates.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: If you had a day job or a little job working and you could gig one or two gigs, you could make a pretty good salary for that week, you know.

124.t: Why McRae never joined Duke: pay compared with other bands
124.s: He says Duke paid too little compared with white-band tenor men, and says Lionel Hampton later paid him top salary.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: And I wanted more money for the musicians, because they had worked their hearts out, you know. On the road -- you know, you'd be working (inaudible) family a long time. It's worth something just to be out there all the time.

124.t: Union scale and pay in the dance school
124.s: The dancing schools drew few name musicians; McRae says fifty dollars a week was good money, with union scale around fifty-five at Chick Webb's.
124.ch: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
124.q: was a thing where you're really working. When you go to work. You're paid and people -- you know, you got to prove -- you got a house full of people there. All these men come out to the place -- the weekend be packed, you know, Friday and Saturday. (Inaudible) packed.

76.t: The Nest's clientele and splitting the tips three ways
76.s: The Nest drew society and big-time pimps; the three-man band split large tips evenly, Zutty bringing home piles of cash. Carrington was last seen in Washington in 1946.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: But this (nest) was a place where a lot of society worked, you know, for them big time acts that were playing in town and all. They came there you know? And as I said before, no blacks can go

76.t: The dog Bring Down bought at Westchester
76.s: Marge says Bring Down is named for spending six of ten dollars on the dog when she needed the rent; Zutty bought him while playing at Westchester with Hawk, Hot Lips, Pee Wee and Fats.
76.ch: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
76.q: But 'bring down', when anything was a bring down that was, they didn't use drag in those days. When Zutty told me he had paid seven dollars for the dog out of ten dollars and I was depending on it for the rent. And I said, seven, I got him for sixty one, and I said, boy is that a bring down. And…

76.t: Opening the Three Deuces with his own band and asking for a raise
76.s: Zutty's band at the Three Deuces had Vernon York, Horace Eubanks, Leonard Bibb and Henry Gordon and lasted a year; Marge made him ask Sam Beer for a raise.
76.q: Yes. Roy came in after that. Because Marge told me, why don't you ask Sam Beer for a raise? And so I finally got up the nerve to do it. Because I told her, I said, all the guys are working just like I am and everything like that. I said, it's alright. But she said, no, ask him for a raise. So I…

77.t: Tips beyond wages and splitting with the waiters
77.s: She earned $17.50 then $35 in wages but hundreds in tips, and secretly dropped bills so waiters could pick them up, to avoid sharing with the musicians.
77.q: Oh, I didn't care about -- they didn't have to give me wages at all. Because I was only making $17.50 a week, you know, wages. And then they finally raised me to $35.00. That was a tremendous salary. Oh, my goodness, $35.00, that was a big salary. I used to get $20 bills and $50 bills, and listen,…

77.t: Dreamland's barker Jones, cash pay and income tax
77.s: A barker named Jones hollered outside Dreamland like a circus. Bottoms paid in cash on time with no withholding tax; later she paid her income tax faithfully because she feared the police.
77.q: holler. "Come in and" -- holler like we were a circus inside, you know. He was a mess, Jones was. Yeah, but he finally got married.

77.t: Johnny Kerry books her into Gibson's Standard Theater for $600
77.s: Kerry of the Nest Club books her at John Gibson's theaters in Philadelphia for $600 a week as a blues headliner.
77.q: New York, uh-huh. And a fellow named Johnny Kerry booked me into John Gibson's theater. The theater called The Standard. Got me my first $600.00 a week.

103.t: Tips, the kitty and the $17.50 wage
103.s: Hinton asks about the slang for tips; Jones explains the kitty and splitting tips.
103.q: You put that in the kitty and you had the kitty up with the light in it and the people passed by - they'd just split up the kitty, you know, and you had the two sabrettes around there and you had to take them checks and shake them up because they put the stuff all down in their bosom and all that.

103.t: Birdland small group and Morris Levy's pay
103.s: Jones names Buddy DeFranco, Freddie Green and Joe Shulman in a Birdland group and says Morris Levy paid above union scale.
103.q: Yes, Buddy DeFranco and the bass player that played with tape on his hand - Jimmy Lewis, and Freddie Green. Freddie Green was playing with Lester Young at the Birdland, and Joe Shulman -

103.t: Little Rock at Sam Baker's: short pay, a pawned bass drum and heating the head
103.s: At Sam Baker's in Little Rock he was paid $5 instead of $14 to cover the previous drummer's debt, and had to warm his bass drum by a stove.
103.q: Yes, and we supposed to get $14 a week and I worked 3 weeks before Basie gave me $5, and I pulled out my pistol and I was going to shoot everybody. I had a bass drum that I had to haul off the band and go over to a great big pot-bellied stove to heat it up so it could tighten up so I could finish…

248.t: Tom Anderson's place and tips from Norwegian sailors; goodbye
248.s: Dawson describes the Basin and Iberville place, bandmates Tom Brown and Sam Moran, tips and gold pieces from sailors; the interview closes.
248.ch: Uptown versus downtown styles and Tom Anderson's
248.q: His place was say a ball, a ballroom you know. And he didn't have much of a dancing space there. About in the Corner of Basin. About in Corner of Basin. About in Corner of Basin in된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된 ! About there you say there after된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된 ! About there you say there after된된된된된된된된된된된된된…

248.t: Which halls paid tips: Hunts and Nagel's, Mama Lou's, West End
248.s: Dawson says he made tips only at Hunts and Nagel's, Harry Parker's and the lakefront places with small bands; heavy-band dances were fixed price.
248.q: I never made no tips though. Only, only halls I made tips was, uh, was, uh, Hanson Nagel, and the Rays in Ivorville, Harry Parker, uh, Saratoga, uh, Saratoga and, uh, Ivorville. Billy Phillips was on, uh, Saratoga near the next corner of, uh, uh, uh, uh, more near Benville.

174.t: Pay and bosses at the opera house after the Silver Slipper
174.s: He compares Silver Slipper pay with the $6 scale at the opera house, recounts proving he could read, and lists the owners he played for.
174.ch: Dance jobs and the opera house
174.q: Getting back to that, when I first went to the opera house, I went with, it was Paul Moyer, and the Sam Hopkins playing piano. I told him I wasn't gonna rest him for a couple of weeks, but right with the Silver Slipper, was just making so much money, just making, oh, I guess, $40, $50, $90, $90,…

174.t: Playing multiple funerals a day and pay
174.s: Dejan explains how three funerals in a day were possible because Catholic funerals were short, while Baptist ones ran for hours. He recalls the pay of a dollar and a half a round, long processions past the deceased's bar, and charging double for two-way parades.
174.q: It would last four hours. I don't see how you could play three in one day. Yeah. You see, the Catholic funerals never last long. Oh. You see, if you get two Catholic funerals in the morning and one o'clock, maybe one, two o'clock, you're playing a Baptist or Protestant funeral, well you'd probably…

627.t: Pay for playing fife and fiddle
627.s: Cage says he earned two or three dollars a night for playing, since nobody paid much.
627.ch: Cage in Louisiana, minstrels and learning fiddle
627.q: Oh, I'd get two, three dollars maybe. One dollar or something like that a night. They didn't pay nobody much.

627.t: Money earned since touring began in 1964
627.s: Williams says he earned good money since Newport in 1964, then travelling to San Francisco, New York and overseas, though he still earns $1.40 an hour at his job.
627.ch: Williams on hard times and money
627.q: Oh, yes, sir. I made some money since then. I made plenty of money since then. But I never have got over $1.40 or $1.50 for now. That's all.

22.t: Signorelli, Memphis Five, and Reisenweber's Broadway years
22.s: La Rocca recalls the Margie plug dispute, hiring Frank Signorelli, how the Memphis Five copied the band's arrangements, and the 1917 Reisenweber's engagement, money and clientele.
22.ch: Original Dixieland Jazz Band in New York
22.q: Well, we forgot about Lytel and Frankie Signorelli. About 1920, Signorelli joined my band. At that time they may have had a Memphis Five, but I never heard of them stopping the machine. Well, I had a little bit of friction with Roberson. He had promised the band a thousand dollars if I put Margie…

22.t: A cooperative band of friends, and the two-beat style
22.s: The band split money five ways with LaRocca as business manager; records played; March syncopated style.
22.ch: Band in New York and London
22.q: We had no enemies. It was a cooperative band, and the money was split equally. I did all the business for the band. I did the leading on getting the jobs, and everything else was my job. And when it came to splitting the money up, it was a five-way split. There's some of the boys still living.…

189.t: Pay with Hampton, Basie and Lloyd Price
189.s: Nightly wages, hotel and meals paid by sidemen.
189.q: Well, I'm ashamed to say it, but at that time the money wasn't like it is now. When I first went away with Lionel Hampton, I was making nineteen dollars a night. Now that nineteen dollars, if you just work one week, I mean one night, you just got nineteen dollars. Then, after I left, I started,…

189.t: Hampton and Woody Herman hire cheap young players
189.s: Leaders hire high school musicians who work cheaply.
189.ch: Basie and life on the road
189.q: Basically, he'll hire somebody, he knows what they can do. He's going to take somebody out, Lionel Hamlin's band, or take somebody out of one of those bands. But Lionel will go to high school and get some guys and tutor them.

283.t: Second reel: pay at Toro's and the Grunewald Hotel
283.s: Allen asks what clubs paid; Pecora says about $35 a week at Toro's and $20 plus tips at the Grunewald with Johnny DeDroit.
283.ch: Reel two to four: pay, tailgate and style
283.q: Oh, yeah, well, I played the Groomall Hotel, at Roosevelt Hotel now, with Johnny Deidre, I only got $20. I think it was from $10.30 to $1, $20 a week. But we made tips. We had made with.

283.t: Working many jobs a day with Sharkey for little money
283.s: They talk about banana boat, radio, Blue Room and Famous Door jobs, long hours, and being cheated of the gate.
283.ch: Return to New Orleans and Sharkey
283.q: Yeah, yeah, see. And, uh, then the radio program, I was once a week, then we'd have the jam session. On a Sunday, but we was off on Sundays, see.

288.t: Maple Leaf management; society jobs and lawn parties
288.s: He lists places like country clubs and private parties played, which paid a dollar and a half.
288.q: He was the manager? Yeah, the bass player. And might as well say I was the manager because everything they had to consult with when we went to Shreveport. That's right.

288.t: Storyville audiences and tips thrown by sailors
288.s: Customers applauded and threw money; Charles recalls Celestin making $35 a night in tips.
288.q: They did applaud. Believe me you start playing and they stay right there until you stop playing. Is that right? Oh my goodness.

127.t: How far Punch's trumpet carried and dances at National Park
127.s: Punch says his horn could be heard a mile, and describes playing for dances at National Park under Jack Carey for about $15 each.
127.ch: Money, touring and the loud horn
127.q: You know all. That was Third and Willow. It's a school there now, big school. But it used to be a great big baseball park, see. And we didn't have nothing but a little shit over us. What did you play? Concerts or for dances? Dancers. For dances, huh? Yeah. She'd be loaded at them. Well, who would…

127.t: Living on the levee and playing three nights a week for $2
127.s: Hanging around the levee to avoid plantation work, playing three nights a week for a dollar and a half to two dollars.
127.q: See with me a lot of us hang around that dick I tell you. See out there on them farms if you didn't work you couldn't stay there see. But when you get on by him out there on that levee couldn't nobody bother you. Nothing but the sheriff and if you just tell him you're just laying off or you're sick…

293.t: Playing at Lufkin's and Oakshire's, tips and pay
293.s: Hired Earl Wiggins at a club where he played banjo, got $6 a night plus tips, was fired by the owner, and played at Oakshire's with Johnny Sensei.
293.q: Yeah, well I hired him, you see what I mean? I hired him. Because I was playing piano down there. But the trouble is when I was playing the piano down there, we couldn't get a guitar player nowhere. So what I've done, I hired Wiggins and I played the banjo.

293.t: Playing the parlor and Decatur Street, ending at the Virginia Kitchen
293.s: He tells of a poorly paid job at the parlor, playing Decatur Street dives and ending each night at the Virginia Kitchen.
293.ch: Violinists, Jimmy Noon and Decatur Street
293.q: He was playing with different fellas, you know. Yeah. Around here one time, musicians make the best of the time. Yeah. My father come got me, Frank. Frank come got me one night, knocked on my door. He said, Frank, you got no job tonight. I said, where you playing? He played at the parlor. You know…

298.t: Working the Last Round in the Quarter for tips
298.s: Played nights at a Quarter joint; the salary was tiny but tips of four or five dollars a night made it worthwhile.
298.q: We used to go to work at 10, knock off at 5, 6, 7 o'clock in the morning. Wasn't making what a dollar a night. Plus Tips.

298.t: Rough Decatur Street and 75 cents a night
298.s: Decatur was rough, with fights; he recalls earning 75 cents a night and a raise from the boss.
298.q: Yeah. During that time, those Chong brothers, you might have heard of them Ralph Chong and a whole bunch of them out there. They used to go to clubs picking fights and all those people out there. But things was reasonable. Of course the money wasn't good. Wasn't making no money out there. I tell…

15.t: How cabaret pay worked: requests from singers and tips
15.s: Bands got little solo time since money came from tips for numbers the singers requested; Howard recalls $56 a week plus tips.
15.ch: Chicago in the 1920s: Bix, Armstrong, Morton
15.q: And you see you only had maybe one of, maybe I'll say three or four numbers to do it if you did any at all, but them girls would get requests you know. And that's where the money's coming from. Unless somebody requests a number and pay for it and the girls didn't know it, that's when the band would…

15.t: Elgar band personnel, summer pier dances and wages
15.s: Howard names Cliff King, Buster Bailey and a clarinetist named Lane in the 22-piece band, the Municipal Pier dances, and his pay of $56 a week.
15.q: Oh, yeah. Well, they had arrangements, you know, and things like that. And the guy took a solo. He just took a solo. You know who was in that band? You've heard of Cliff King, the Clannett player, haven't you? Yeah. And Buster Bailey. Yeah. They had another fellow from New Orleans named Lane. I…

304.t: Parties, passing the hat and tips
304.s: Wood never attended student parties with bands and saw no collections at parades, only tips at the Paddock Lounge.
304.ch: French Quarter music, then and now
304.q: Well, if they did, I was a married graduate student, and I don't remember ever going to a party, You didn't go to a party with a band? Where there was live music, no, no.

304.t: Union status and pay for brass band jobs
304.s: They discuss whether bands were union and what Casimir and Young Tuxedo were paid, five or ten dollars, with funeral rates.
304.ch: Return in 1965, pay and Preservation Hall
304.q: I didn't know any of them were unions then.

202.t: Prices of movies, vaudeville and club dates
202.s: Movie and vaudeville ticket prices, and a comparison with what young players earn on club dates today.
202.q: Oh gee, well now we used to call it a nickelette. So that was just the movies. But a vaudeville show was probably about 25 or 30 cents or something. I know it’s hard to believe. Well whenever anybody says — you know these young fellas, they go out and they do these club dates, and I says well how—…

202.t: Prohibition-era pay, tips, the union, and the Sherwood Inn
202.s: Early jobs paid a few dollars but tips could be large; as leader he earned $35 a week seven nights after the union came in, and he later ran the Sherwood Inn in New Hyde Park.
202.q: Well it’s different areas. When I first went out I was, there was days when everything was illegal. There was no liquor, so it was prohibition. So everything I went with, even club dates, if they served liquor illegal so the girls, we used to have a kitty. And we’d have three pieces, like a…

606.t: Pay in the early years with Gray, Dorsey and Peterson
606.s: Ellis recalls $175 a week with Dorsey, a raise with Oscar, and touring Europe with Jazz at the Philharmonic in good hotels.
606.ch: Pay, health and the Gibson guitar
606.q: In the earlier years? Well I was with Glen Grey, you probably don’t even remember that name but that was an orchestra, and they played pretty well. And then when I went with Jimmy I made more and this is back in the ‘40s, you know, the early ‘40s. And I finally got to making, now this will seem…

606.t: Working for Norman Granz and pay of $500 a week
606.s: Granz was a great businessman who wouldn't give a mid-tour raise; Ellis joined in 1953 at $500 a week.
606.ch: Jazz at the Philharmonic and Norman Granz
606.q: He was wonderful. Great businessman. And he had certain rules. I remember one time I didn’t think I was getting enough money so I asked Norman for a raise. And he said, “You know better than that,” he said, “I can’t give you a raise in mid-tour.” He said, “Before the next tour we’ll negotiate.”

542.t: Touring Australia and pay of about $60 a week
542.s: The band toured northern Australia and the Outback; he played bebop on Sundays and earned about $60 a week.
542.q: And we did tours of Northern Australia and the Outback. And it was great. So we got to see the country up on the Great Barrier Reef.

542.t: Money with Maynard and saving on the road
542.s: He did not haggle over pay, following his parents' advice; Maynard paid hotels and he saved money traveling like a tourist.
542.q: No. No. My parents had always said to me, because there was a huge recession in New Zealand when gasoline was rationed and all this kind of stuff. And a lot of people were unemployed. And when I was of employable age, my parents said, “if you get a job, be thankful you’ve got the job and work out…

226.t: Scale wages, first real money with Shearing, and the gift of a bass
226.s: Pay was small; Levy's real money came with Shearing; after he stopped playing, Nancy and Joe gave him a bass for his 75th birthday.
226.q: Well I know I worked, I worked in night clubs in Chicago coming along and made $50 a week, and that was, that was big money, you know? It wasn’t big money, it was just enough to get by on, but my first experience of really making money was really with George Shearing because up to that point, even…

226.s: The contract paid about $400 a week for 40 weeks, with long hours and sitting in at nearby clubs between sets.
226.q: Oh yeah. It did, and the period was contracted for. It was a longer period that I had anything happen in Chicago or any place else. The money was substantial.

514.t: Hampton's all-star alumni and his pay of 165 dollars a week
514.s: Mabern and Rowe discuss the stars who passed through Hampton's band and what it paid, 165 a week, of which he saved 100.
514.q: He didn’t pay good. Well but let’s face it though, but he paid what was the going rate during that time, because I know they’d give you money in this envelope and they’d have all the deductions. It was 165 a week. But after the 165 I was able to save a hundred dollars. You see what I’m saying? So…

514.t: Chicago pay scale and saving for New York
514.s: A weekend gig at 45 dollars a night was good money; he banked it to fund the move to New York.
514.q: Well if you made, say if you made 45 dollars on a weekend, that was a lot of money. If you made a gig, like a private party where you made 75 or a 100 dollars, oh man, that was fantastic. But I would say the basic pay would be something like 45 dollars per night. And what I would do is I would get…

609.t: Pearl Bailey on musicians pricing themselves out; club costs
609.s: May recalls Pearl Bailey's views on musicians leaving to lead bands, and discusses club costs and just wanting to play.
609.ch: Mingus, road life and the jazz economy
609.q: It is. It’s very expensive. If you don’t put a hundred bucks in your pocket, you might not have enough, to take your wife out, just to go to the club, not to have dinner and all that. So it’s pretty expensive. And I remember Pearl Bailey told — I used to fill in for Milt Hinton when Milt couldn’t…

609.t: Day job, Birdland and generosity with money
609.s: Billy Taylor's Birdland offer led May to leave an insurance day job; he earned more on weekends and tells how he tips freely.
609.ch: Billy Taylor years and the greats
609.q: Oh yeah. I’ll tell you why, because not being trained at all, not playing the bass left handed like that, I couldn’t study formally or anything like that. So I just wound up saying to myself I’m going to have a day job during the week, I don’t know, five days a week or whatever, and I’ll work on…

162.t: Eighty-five dollars a week was big money
162.s: He says the pay was enough to support his family and send money home.
162.q: Oh that was big money. Gee if you got the hundred dollars, you know a dollar was a dollar then. So that fifteen dollars, to get to a hundred, wow.

162.t: Joining Harry James in 1939 and what the job paid
162.s: He sat in at the rehearsal and was hired; pay was eighty-five dollars, the same as with Norvo.
162.q: From Red Norvo, yeah. Well, like Jerry Jerome said, “Harry James is having a rehearsal, so go up there,” which I did. And he says, “You got your trumpet with you?” I says, “Yeah.” I always went in town with the horn you know. And he says, “All right, after we take a break” he says, “you want to…

585.t: Pay at New York clubs and young players working cheap
585.s: Hundred-dollar gigs have not risen in years; she objects to college kids playing for next to nothing.
585.ch: Work, pay and the New York life
585.q: Well I don’t really do any gigs under a hundred bucks. And there are a lot of hundred buck gigs and they have stayed a hundred bucks for a very long time. You know what I mean? So the pay hasn’t gone up in New York in a very long time. You could go as low as, my goodness, my sister did a gig there…

585.t: Logistics and pay of corporate gigs in Manhattan
585.s: Hauling a PA and bass into midtown, parking, and corporate gigs paying $300 or more.
585.ch: Work, pay and the New York life
585.q: You can say that. I don’t know how many gigs I’ve done in midtown where you really have to call someone. “I need help.” Sometimes I have to take a PA, particularly if they want me to sing and play the whole night. So you’ve got a PA, an acoustic bass and an amplifier and the gig is upstairs at the…

396.t: Big band pay, rehearsal bands and the union
396.s: Big bands pay $10-15 unless there is a grant; rehearsal bands at the union on 48th Street play for free; classical players are more rigid about pay.
396.q: Well when you have a grant it’s pretty easy. Other than that it’s just about impossible. Most of the big bands around town, they work for $10, $15 dollars and I just can’t ask people to do that.

396.t: What New York clubs pay and an exploitative Sunday offer
396.s: Clubs pay little or nothing; she turned down a job running Sunday shows for a percentage of the door; New Jersey and Connecticut pay somewhat better.
396.q: It’s true. I mean there’s so many great jazz musicians. They come from all over the world and then the students graduating from the colleges, and the clubs really do know that they have a free meal. So they tend not to pay union scale. There may be one that does, I don’t know. And some will just…

108.t: Local pay and promoters who avoided paying bands
108.s: Wilder first earned three or four dollars a night; stories of the Gorham band's pay and of clubs claiming the money had been stolen.
108.q: In Philadelphia, I think it was – when I was coming in, when I first started, it was $3 or $4 a night. We’re talking playing four hours, three or four hours a night. I remember one time creating some real disturbance in one band. We were all driving. They had three cars to transport Jimmy Gorham’s…

108.t: Slave wages and treating other musicians fairly
108.s: Wilder reflects that the pay was poor while the band made a fortune, and says it taught him to split pay equally, as with the Schaefer Beer quartet.
108.q: You could get by on that, but you were also playing your room rent out of that. And it was almost like in a sense I guess you could say we were like slave labor you know, slave wages. And they were making a fortune, I mean really making a fortune. You couldn’t get into the halls where they were…

588.t: Traveling cheaply and what she earned
588.s: She went by bus and car, earned $100 a week in Honolulu, and says the people make musicians rich.
588.ch: Venues, circuits and the music business
588.q: The best we could. By bus, by car. The least expensive way. When I started to make a $100 a week in Honolulu, I thought wow, I didn't know there was all this money in the music, you know. I worked as a maid and I had made like $30 a week which was pretty good for a maid in that time. But I was…

588.t: Beatles pay, jazz pay and money
588.s: She compares the Beatles' pay with Miles Davis's weekly pay and says she doesn't miss money.
588.ch: Venues, circuits and the music business
588.q: And here we were working for -- Miles was making $5,000 a week and he was supposed to be one of the privileged ones. $3,000 a week was good money. This is what they dumped on us, and then after awhile, folks started crossing the barriers and using electricity. People who really knew how to bring…

107.t: Basie pay, raises, family and arranging fees
107.s: He started at $150 a week, reached about $200, doubled in Europe, and relied on $35-50 arrangements and royalties.
107.ch: Joining Basie and life on the road
107.q: Pay must have been pretty good for the veterans, the guys, Marshall Royal and Henry Coker and Joe Newman and Renauld Jones and Freddie Green, of course. To me, one who had not been a professional, but fresh out of the army -- I don’t consider that a professional musician life. New in the industry,…

107.t: One-day trips, $10 pay and Jack Jackson the boxer
107.s: Every trip was there and back in a day, pay topped out at $10 a job, and Jackson was a former pro boxer turned tenor player.
107.ch: Cincinnati bands, race and the road to college
107.q: It wasn’t life on the road per se. Every trip was there and back in one day, Cincinnati being the home base. We went to Chillicothe, we came back. We went to Portsmouth, we came back. We went to Lexington and we came back, except this one night I didn’t come back and missed school the next day. We…

224.t: Pay with Bird in Philadelphia and with Lester Young
224.s: Money often ran out by week's end in Philly; he made about $96 a week with Lester Young.
224.q: When we would play Philadelphia – Bird never stayed in Philly, because he said if he did stay there, he would be arrested. He’d be busted. So he would commute. It would take money to commute. By the end of the week, sometimes there was no money there. The union would be there. The union man would…

224.t: How long with Sabby Lewis, and asking him for pay
224.s: He stayed only weeks, and later wrote Sabby from New York for money owed.
224.ch: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
224.q: When I went to New York, Sabby had owed me some money. I’m big time now. I’m going to New York. I say, “Sabby.” The word was – I was very independent then, even. Just starting, I’m independent. You’re supposed to ask for some money, or more money than they’re paying. I started out doing that with…

123.t: How the Roosevelt sessions were funded
123.s: The sessions were volunteer, with a quarter admission rented basses and drums and the money going to the student fund.
123.ch: Roosevelt jazz sessions and Charlie Parker
123.q: And later the guys started bringing their own stuff. We charged a quarter and it went to the student fund.

123.t: The Jazz Showcase name and the sixties Chicago clubs
123.s: He explains the name, lists clubs where he ran off-night sessions, and says musicians were paid whatever was left.
123.q: I derived the name from my initials of course, JS and jam sessions, and Jazz Showcase. So as I said we did the Gate of Horn, then we started doing stuff up on Rush Street, different places. And then on Wells Street when the hippie era was going in the sixties. We had a place at Mother Blues, at the…

377.t: Pay in the early days and Billie's wages
377.s: Basie describes work for meal tickets and show pay, and refuses to contradict Billie's claim of $125 a week, saying she made more than anyone.
377.ch: Billie Holiday with the band (1971 session)
377.q: Well, it would be like -- (inaudible) if you was with a show and you was getting paid with a meal ticket, something like that, you know, I mean, during the (inaudible) get any money or anything like that [now].

377.t: Billie's daily pay and Jimmy Rushing not lending money
377.s: Kuehl reports Billie's claims about $14 a day and Jimmy Rushing refusing a loan; Basie says he does not know.
377.ch: Billie Holiday with the band (1971 session)

677.t: Salary and five or six shows a day
677.s: He confirms $70 for seven-day weeks versus others' $125, played his solo five or six times daily in theaters, and lived on savings during idle stretches.
677.q: Everybody made the same thing except me. Well, of course, Hardwicke when he came. He didn't make $125.00 either. I don't know exactly what he made, but $70.00 was my salary. And if you worked two days, you got two-sevenths, and if you worked all week you got it all, but --

677.t: Guaranteed salary and who was highest paid
677.s: Brown denies being highest paid and says only a few men were paid whether the band worked, with Hodges higher.
677.ch: Los Angeles scene and the Ellington sound
677.q: Yes, but the amount of the weekly salary was -- I don't think was near Johnny's, which -- rightfully so. Johnny was really a terrific contributor.

17.t: How Cole joined Cab; $150 a week
17.s: Foots Thomas got him in; Cab and Duke paid top salaries.
17.ch: Dancers, Newton, Chu Berry and the Cab Calloway band
17.q: Yeah, Foots Thomas is the one got me on the band. And I didn't want to join the band first because I was having a ball over there on 52nd Street with Stuff. Stuff Smith, small band, and of course, with Cab's band, Cab and Duke then were the highest paid bands out there, which was $100 a week, but…

17.t: Cab's hits and the best-paid band
17.s: 'Hi Di Ho' and 'Jim Jam Jumpin''; Cab and Duke paid $100 a week.
17.ch: Dancers, Newton, Chu Berry and the Cab Calloway band
17.q: Oh yeah, yeah. He and Duke were the highest paid bands out there. And that was the going salary, $100 a week. Everybody jumped at that.

9.s: Sidemen made fifty dollars a week and up, while leaders' earnings depended on what the band took in.
9.ch: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
9.q: : Well, from fifty dollars a week up. Which wasn't bad. Not good, but it wasn't bad. And Willie was making more...Willie's band was making more than that.

9.t: Armstrong's band paid better than Russell's, but Joe Glaser got rich
9.s: Armstrong's fixed nightly pay was steadier than Russell's hit-or-miss dates, though Glaser made far more from Armstrong's name.
9.ch: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
9.q: : Well, with the Russell band we did a lot of hard playing. We didn't draw many people. Consequently, we didn't make much money. And with Louis, we drew a lot of people, but we wasn't gettin' much salary! But the salary we was gettin' was much more than we ever made with Russell's band, because…

381.t: Savoy scale versus Arcadia pay, and Lucky's nightly pay
381.s: The Savoy paid $33 a week against the Arcadia's $50, but Lucky paid $11 a night on tour.
381.q: Yeah, we got paid nightly. And at that time, they were paying like $7 or $8 a night, and Lucky was paying $11, so this was really big time -- he was paying $11 a night.

381.t: Local ballroom gigs and the pay
381.s: The Cavaliers undercut Hartley Toots for ballrooms and clubs and shared about a dollar a man a night.
381.ch: Teenage bands and Florida road tours
381.q: Oh, no; we had a big band, man. We played the ballrooms; we played all of the clubs -- that Hartley Toots wasn't able to play for, and they were able to get us cheaper anyway, so we got a lot of the gigs that Hartley Toots would have been playing. We played at the Elks, [Best.]

641.t: Berger's job terms and paying off Doc Moon
641.s: Berger offered thirty-odd dollars a week plus room, whiskey-making and car-stealing, and Doc Moon furiously accepted his ninety dollars.
641.ch: Southern Illinois roadhouse and St. Louis
641.q: Yeah, so to get back to Charlie... I says, 'Well, what about the money?' He says, 'I'll pay you [what was it?] thirty dollars a week or thirty-five...' -- I can't remember exactly. He says, 'But, I'll give you a place to stay, and we make whiskey here and beer in the daytime, and if you want to…

641.t: Ory's band: professional, no jam sessions
641.s: The Ory band did no day jobs after becoming successful and rarely jammed, except at Buster's house.
641.ch: Joe Liggins and back to Kid Ory
641.q: I used to do a lot of it. And I can't remember Ram doing...and Frank... Well, Frank Passley wasn't in the band anyway. But I'm trying to think... Well, at Buster's house... That's where we all gathered. Buster used to live at 53rd and Central, and that's where... A lot of musicians when they'd…

91.t: Ending the band and Savoy pay scale
91.s: The band ended for lack of dates after about 3 months at the Savoy at $33 a man and $66 for the leader.
91.ch: The Savoy band and the Swing era
91.q: I think that was it. Because I'm wondering if that was in 1933 or 1939 when it was that. Maybe it was still the same in 1939, or maybe it was less in 1933. I'm not sure.

91.t: Carter's band and Henderson's on a par; Roseland security and pay
91.s: Carter thinks Henderson lasted longer because of Roseland's security; he earned $110 a week with Fletcher versus the Savoy's $33 scale.
91.ch: The Savoy band and the Swing era
91.q: Well, I think that probably has to do with Fletcher's ability to keep his band together, you know, longer, at any given time, because of having that security of what we might call a home, quote, unquote, the Roseland Ballroom, you know? As I think of it now, I don't know of any other black band…

71.t: Pay: two dollars a night at the Reno, thirty-three dollars at the Savoy
71.s: After good pay in Shanghai he earned two dollars a night in Kansas City and $33 a week at the Savoy.
71.ch: Back to Los Angeles and joining Basie
71.q: But see, in the Reno Club we worked from ten o'clock at night until four o'clock in the morning. Out of all the salaries I made, I made a nice salary in Shanghai and I had been making some pretty nice salaries. I got to Kansas City, they paid me from ten o'clock to four o'clock in the morning, I…

71.t: Pay and expenses on the road
71.s: With $24 a night, work only a few nights a week and two sets of expenses, musicians like him and Harry Edison could barely save.
71.q: Yes, it is. That goes along with the business. It shouldn't. You don't save much money. You've got to pay two expenses. You've got to pay at home, you've got to keep that going and you've got to pay your hotel and your expenses on the road which can be kind of high. So you can't hardly save very…

93.t: The end of the Buck and Bubbles era and $650 a week apiece
93.s: Bubbles' pneumonia ended the arrangement; the pair moved around hotels and by their peak earned $650 apiece weekly with rising pay.
93.q: Well, I would always get the $250.00, you see. That was sufficient for me, because it was kind of -- the work was kind of steady, because as I say, Chuck and Chuckles was on the increase, from stopping so many shows, you see, and we became the Kennedy favorites, right after that, about a year and a…

93.t: Earning $500 a week and the lifetime contract
93.s: In 1942 the pair earned $500 a week between them, with money going to families and Lucille Achet under the life contract, leaving Green about $250.
93.q: Eventually, Chuck and Chuckles went on further, and we were on another tour. What they call, we was out of our apprenticeship then. We was going on to become stars, which a lot of the show folks were in hopes of happening, because we were getting to be young men then.

388.t: Wartime pay for the triple workload
388.s: Leeman earned $150 for the radio show, $175 at the Roxy and $175 from Kirby, a fabulous sum then, though he got only a few hours of sleep.
388.ch: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
388.q: Well, this is late '44-'45, this was during the thick of the war and money was very loose, nobody was keeping too many records -- except CBS.

388.s: Hinton explains for the record the tip box tradition and asks Leeman to talk about Harold West and Clyde Hart.

30.t: Earning more after Duke, and the raise he won in 1930
30.s: He made more money after leaving Duke and most with Louie, whose overhead was smaller, while Duke and Irving Mills kept the money and refused raises; he once quit in New York to get one.
30.ch: Leaving Duke and the Hollywood years
30.q: Oh, yeah. I made more money after I left Duke than I did with Duke, period. And I made more money than both of them when I went with Louie. Duke couldn't pay me the salary that Louie paid me, or he wouldn't and I wouldn't

30.t: Luis Russell's band at the Nest Club and the Broadway tips
30.s: He joined Luis Russell at the Nest Club, working ten to six or seven in the morning for Broadway stars like Helen Morgan and Harry Richman; salary was $84 a week with tips almost as much.
30.q: So then from then -- Then, getting back to New York, one night I went to work with Luis Russell at a place called The Nest Club, and I worked with Luis Russell for a long time.

31.t: A $500 colonial costume gig in Worcester and a cancelled job
31.s: A Harvard student hires Whaley's four-man band for $500 at a colonial party where they barely play, and later a false telegram cancelling a job is settled by his lawyer.
31.q: And I was playing down on Beech Street, and a Harvard student came in one night and he says, 'hey, how much you charge to play down in Worcester?' I said, '$500,' just like that, see. Now, I didn't know -- I thought he was kidding, see, so I said $500. I had four men there. So about a couple of…

31.t: Pay and bandmates at Suntaug Lake Inn
31.s: He explains pay rose from room and board to $250-300 a week, and names Carl White, Leroy Tibbs, Clarence Cummings and Willie Lynch.
31.ch: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
31.q: But all them people come down here today and they tip $10. Man, you know, we used to make $35 a night -- five of us, and we each made $35 a night.

529.t: Bradshaw's pay, $35 a night, and learning to be a professional
529.s: Bradshaw carries a safe in his car trunk and pays $35 a night against $22 elsewhere.
529.ch: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
529.q: Yeah. And the--and the--and those road bands, you didn't get but twenty-two dollars a night. Bradshaw paid thirty-five--

529.t: Demanding more than $50 a week and walking out
529.s: The band, paid $50 a week, asks for a raise, is threatened with being unable to play anywhere, and skips the weekend.
529.q: OK, so after a while--we went on with that. So I went and asked the man--said "look here, man. We done built your--built this business up. Now we want some more money." He was paying us like $50 a week. $50 a week. Working--working six nights a week. We was only off on Mondays. And you know, well,…

13.t: Other New Orleans players, pay and hours in the cabarets
13.s: He names Ory, Dutrey and Dominique; pay was $35-40 a week for six-hour nights.
13.q: I don't even remember what year that was. Must have been in between the time -- between Milwaukee engagements.

13.t: Money on the road and raising four daughters
13.s: About $10 a night with little tax; theater scale was $73.
13.q: It was in the thirties. But that was during the Depression. You didn't have unions -- didn't have all that union tax to pay. Only tax we had to pay was like the -- the scales in the town we were playing in might be 50 cents or 60 cents.

112.t: Tips and singers in the cabarets
112.s: Albertson asks about tips; Wooding says he was not yet playing for singers, and that singers split tips with the band.
112.q: : OH. Well, we hadn't worked up to no singers.

112.s: He earned twenty dollars at best, much lost to tabs, and jokes about not making a pimp.
112.q: : At the Bucket of Blood? Well, I was lucky if I got twenty-five dollars, or twenty dollars. But, and I didn't get all of that, because we'd tab half of that up because the rest of your friends would all come in and say, alright what

172.t: Managing musicians and what the dances paid
172.s: Handling difficult players, then pay rates from the Silver Leaf days to the Tuxedo Band.
172.q: When we first started playing, we used to play all around, all the little white dance and everything like that, ten dollars and a half. Three hours.
