173.t: Pay for parades and dances, and hard-drinking musicians
173.s: Jobs paid about three dollars; he kept his day job, unlike Gitsall and Galaty who played for drinks.
173.q: same as that about the same yeah so it wouldn't pay you to go to work and neglect something that you was following up as a means of livelihood you understand it wouldn't pay to neglect that to go fool around playing music but there's plenty fellas that's all they thought of now like Willie Gitsall…

402.t: Pay at the Fern; Buzzy Willow takes over the band
402.s: Sal explains $40 a week pay at the Fern and how Buzzy Willow became leader.
402.q: I didn't get into the job. I said, Goppsen, oh, he's a great drummer. Which he is. But the guy said, he got a break with B-Funk. I mean, the guy's a top-knop musician, man. He can play with anybody. How much did they pay at the fern? I'm always wondering. Well, I'll tell you that story, too. I'll…

621.t: Getting jobs, pay and places played
621.s: Engagements came by cards and phone at $2.75 a man for four hours; he lists Storyville cabarets, hotels and out-of-town towns.
621.q: Well, I'll tell you, the, the leader of the band usually have cards made, and, and a phone number. So naturally, when they want you, they phone you, that, uh, they got an engagement for you. Then the price is as usual, $2.75 a man. That's what you got in the night, but four hours work, from eight…

862.t: Pay for funerals and how it was spent
862.s: Funeral pay is five to seven dollars with the leader getting more; it was two dollars when he arrived. He spent much on drink and also played nightly dances.
862.q: Well, they pay, I believe, six to five dollars, six to five or seven dollars, seven dollars. I know when they went out, you know, they're going to give you six dollars on the man, except the leader, of course, you know, they get more.

178.t: Good jobs, bad jobs and early pay and tips
178.s: He lists high-class jobs with Pichon and beer-garden gigs that paid almost nothing, such as a dollar and a half a night.
178.q: Well I played some nice jobs because I've seen, I played, when I was with Walter Pichot, we played at the Jung, played at the Roosevelt, played at the Roseanne Restaurant, played at I think it's, I don't know if it was on the one, we played at the Country Club. Those are all nice jobs. I mean of…

179.t: Not in Peter's orchestra; Navy day job and parade pay
179.s: Low pay made him stop; he worked at the Navy and took days off for funerals and parades with the Excelsior at about thirty dollars.
179.q: Well I was waking down at the Navy at that time. Oh. Yes, waking at the government. Of course I could get off, go play funerals and parades like that, because I had days up there that I could take off and go play parades and things like that. We used to play the longshoremen parades, lab-a-dee…

724.t: Whether music pays; wages and jukeboxes
724.s: Music is worth it to him; pay was about a dollar an hour, and jukeboxes later cut into the work.
724.ch: Buddy Petit, Kid Thomas and working life
724.q: It's a little late now. I want to ask you something. Do you think playing music is worth it? Or not? Well, it's worth it to me. I mean, it seems like you had to study hard and work hard on it. It was worth it back then, huh? Yeah. Just getting a wire guy to play his music. It's worth it. I think…

827.t: Band pay in the old days
827.s: Musicians earned about a dollar and a half a night and a band could be hired for fifteen dollars.
827.q: Today, when you pay one man to play now, you could get a whole band for it in them times.

773.t: Marriage in 1913; husband's jobs, Cadillac pay, the kitty can, wartime wages and radio
773.s: His day jobs, $25 a week and tips at the Cadillac, the kitty can, a dollar a night in the French Quarter in World War I, and the family radio with Louis Armstrong.
773.ch: Arnold DePass's life and the Cadillac years
773.q: Yeah, he come up with my brothers, you know.

624.t: The slaughterhouse, five-dollar day and Mrs. Brunies on brother Abbie
624.s: Allen asks about the slaughterhouse where they played, a long Mardi Gras day for five dollars, and Mrs. Brunies recalls brother Abbie playing in clubs.
624.ch: Playing in clubs and Mardi Gras
624.q: Yeah. Well, it's that way down. It's far enough, but it's... It's about the 1,600 blocks. About 1,600. 1,600 below Canale's there. It's about 1,600. 800, 1,700.

258.t: Pay, sleeping arrangements and unions on the shows
258.s: Sleepers were free, meals paid for, salaries began at $25 a week, and union and non-union men were mixed.
258.ch: Rabbit Foot show and show life
258.q: You had sleepers. They had sleepers on these train shows. Your sleeping was free, but you ate at the dining car. You paid for what you ate. At that time, salaries were ranging from $25 a week up.

626.t: Yearly bookings, more organizations and typical pay
626.s: Groups signed the band up a year ahead; the interviewer reads out more clients (clubs, shipbuilders, churches) and pay of about $2-4 a job.
626.q: Now, you see, people in order to get the Excelsior Band, draw a crowd, they did sign up jobs with us sometimes from this year to the next year, you see. Take that same date on a big holiday or something like that. All the people that we'd play for regularly, you know, they'd sign up from one year…

647.t: Pay at house parties and playing old numbers for white parties
647.s: Pay of three to five dollars with no tips, but tips from white patrons for old standards.
647.q: No, no tips. No tips. Now, when we would play some of, for some of the white people, you'd make tips. Sometimes a fellow would actually play Satan numbers, they wanted all the old numbers that you could think of, like after the ball was over, down by the old mill stream, so they could get a, what…

864.t: Pay with Kid Thomas and all-night work for a dollar
864.s: He made more money with Thomas than any band, out-of-town work for $8 to $10 before the union; elsewhere he played all night for a dollar.
864.q: Well, yeah, like I said, I played with Thomas. I made more money with him than any band I played with. How kind of money did you make? Did Kips, you mean? Well, in average it was more money but less money. You see, the skills wasn't like it is now. We wasn't in the union. And we was making around…

903.t: Longer engagements at Mama Lou's during the Depression and after army
903.s: He describes steady Saturday and holiday work at Mama Lou's, pay and tips, raising the price after the army, and a drunk captain offering a hundred dollar bill.
903.q: Well, the longer engagements, let me see, I was at the Humming Boy and then out at Mamalu. But after I went to the army and come back I went out there and worked. And the time we was working out there, before the war, we was getting about two and a half a man out of tips. But the tips was great.…

38.t: Wickliffe as bandleader and the Windsor Theater job
38.s: Wickliffe was a good talker who got good men and good pay, including a Windsor Theater job paying $45 a week.
38.q: Smart enough to get the right men, yeah. He always had a good band. And he was a good talker and getting jobs. And when he got a good job, he could always come around and say, I got a good job. He's paying so much money a week. And I want a good trumpet player and something like that. He would get…

266.t: Salary and the cooperative arrangement in the Basin Street Six
266.s: Jones earned $100 a week against a scale near $56, as the only non-owner of a cooperative band, with Joe Rodas handling the mic.
266.q: It was, uh, I went on the Basin Street Six, and it was a terrific salary at that time. I was making a hundred dollars a week. It's 1953, huh? 52, 53, I guess. When, uh, when, uh, scale, when musicians was only about fifty-eight dollars a week, fifty-six dollars a week. And I was the lowest paid…

268.s: Turner talks about prices for band jobs and uniforms.
268.ch: Day job, war and Bocage's band
268.q: Well yeah. They had to, the type of people that was playing with, you know, playing for, you're playing with this and Price was a man thing. For instance if you, I'll go there, if Price was ranging for six pieces, say about $80, they would consider you a good band, you see, it was too cheap. You go…

620.t: Why house parties were held and how little they paid
620.s: House parties were for fun, with a nickel at the door; rent was a few dollars a month yet money was scarce, and he often played for nothing.
620.q: No, I don't believe it was for the rent. I believe the people would do it more for the fun of us. Yeah. Give them the part of that. Get the children to pay to put the nickel up to come in. There would be a hoobah nickel to go in. Yeah. You know? Them chicks would come in and sell pop and, uh,…

873.t: Pay for funerals and dance jobs, and what he earned
873.s: Funeral bands play free; Lawrence earned $2.50 when starting and $7-8 later, spending more on music than he made.
873.q: Not on music, no. Just on the other part, huh? Well the music, you know, it's kind of money for them. They're always free, you know, the bands are always free. They're never to charge for the music for a funeral anyway. They were always free.

653.t: Dew Drop owners and the eight and twelve dollar pay scale
653.s: The Panniers ran the Dew Drop; musicians were paid either eight or twelve dollars a night depending on reading ability.
653.q: Here comes Pat. And, uh, that was at the Dewdrop. Now, the Dewdrop, I don't know how many stories you've heard about the Dewdrop and how it, uh, was in operation. But it was run by, uh, three brothers, mainly by Frank Pannier, uh, Joe Pannier and his brother, uh, Paul. Paul. Paul. Paul. Paul fed…

765.t: Pay at the Legion: percentage deal versus union scale
765.s: Percentage deal, union scale of $13, and the cover charge.
765.ch: Buck's Legion band and later gigs
765.q: They were, well, planes. Sometimes a dollar, a dollar and a half. And they were on a commission. And then the war broke out. They were, was making between $25 and $30 a man a night. Was that from the kiddie? No, just from the kiddie. It was a 60-40 deal.

275.s: A dollar and a half a night was top pay and twenty-five dollars a week made you a headliner.
275.q: Well, when I started out, a dollar and a half a night was top salary. And when you got twenty-five dollars a week, well, you were a headliner.

276.t: Mirrors at Spano's and Savocas; pay and Sweet Lucy wine
276.s: Comparison of Spano's mirror with Savocas, band size, and musicians paid with a few hours and all the wine they could drink.
276.q: Yeah, that's right. It had a mirror, a long mirror, because all the women that's coming in and dancing, they all would look to see themselves dancing. That big, long mirror in there.

734.t: Pay in the country: six dollars a night
734.s: Pay was six dollars a man a night; he earlier worked in the field for two bits a day.
734.q: We was getting six dollars a night. Six dollars a man. Six dollars a man. Wasn't bad, wasn't it? No. We already got a dollar and a half a night in the district. That was big money, see. I got two and a half a night on Saturday night when I first started playing. That's all I got. And could live a…

277.t: Paid jobs, Mandel Hall concert, and Baby Dodds on Lovett's Dodds style
277.s: The band played fraternity jobs and a Mandel Hall benefit with Art Hodes, Baby Dodds and Preston Jackson; Dodds praised his Johnny Dodds-like style.
277.ch: University of Chicago and the Cakewalking Babies
277.q: G-E-R-O-U-L-D. Yeah, I think we played a few jobs. I can't, I think we played some fraternity house jobs at the university and things like that. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. I remember we played a concert at Mandel Hall. I think it was a benefit for the United Negro College Fund. G-E-R-O-U-L-D. And Art Hodes was…

569.s: He says street advertising paid a dollar to a dollar and a quarter, plus pay from the dance itself.
569.q: Is that, oh my God, you want me to say this? Well, I tell you, at that time I have, uh, got no more than, uh, for advertising. Sometime you got a dollar and a quarter. Sometime you got a dollar. For the advertising.

44.t: Washboard and percussion, Maxey's band earnings and twin sister

You know what I do? You know what I do? You just hit it with just everything. I get off there. That's right. The most…

628.s: Williams explains how the band advertised the fights and then played at the Coliseum and Hyman Park between rounds for six dollars a night.
628.q: And then we used to, I had all them fights. We used to play all the fights. Oh, yeah? Yeah. How did that work? Oh, we used to advertise for the fight. Mm-hmm. Back on the same day. Mm-hmm.

629.t: Playing nightly in the District for tips and pay
629.s: After a question on marriage, Picou describes eight-to-four shifts at a dollar and a quarter, no dancing, requests, and a $50 tip.

1026.t: Raising admission to fifty cents and a dollar
1026.s: Recollections of the price going up, enforcing it at the door, and a story of a band returning to find they had to pay.

So, you know, it was always, you know, sort of, I felt bad, you know, walking in front of the band and asking for…

190.t: Playing with Chris Kelly, Sam Morgan and Buddy Petit as a money musician
190.s: He played with Chris Kelly, Sam Morgan and Buddy Petit; he would play with anyone paying; only Clayton cheated him.
190.q: I was a money musician, see? Yeah. Yeah. I played with all my brothers, man. My brothers couldn't get nobody, they'd come get me, you know. They were scared to ask me, you know, if I wouldn't play, you know. I said, shoot, man, I'd play with anybody that got some money. All the money musicians,…

191.t: Pay at the Hotel Edson in Beaumont, commonwealth bands and a New Orleans agent
191.s: Kelly's 1930 seven-piece band got room for $2.75 a week and ten dollars for Saturday night; the leader's workload and a New Orleans booking agent are discussed.
191.q: Um, I had a band in 1930 that was a real good little band, seven piece band, and we stayed at the Hotel Edson in Beaumont, Texas. Uh-huh. Two dollars and seventy-five cents each per week. And we played every Saturday night on the roof. Uh-huh. And that was the only guarantee that we had. The rest…

182.t: Parade pay and long carnival days with Grand Isle trips
182.s: Funerals paid $3 and parades up to $5, while carnival paid $10 a man.
182.q: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. $3 for a funeral and most you could get is $5 for a parade. Now like on the place for the bulls, not the bulls to El Noro, but we paid us $10.

819.t: The red light district, supervised cabarets and tips
819.s: How the district was divided, how Sbarbaro's side was run, and pay by tips.

777.t: Sonny Williams Jazz Band contract form from 1927
777.s: Allen reads the printed band contract; Williams explains deposits, balance and that the leader also managed the band.
777.q: We pay so much on the job. Mm-hmm. But deposit on the job. A deposit and then.

139.t: Delivery boy at the drugstore for twelve years
139.s: He worked twelve years as a delivery boy for a store, paid four dollars a week plus all the ice cream he wanted.
139.q: I worked for him twelve years. Twelve years? Wow. Twelve years. I've seen all his churn raised up. Uh-huh.

877.t: Money then versus now; first New Orleans bands
877.s: Handy compares kid earnings with today, then lists playing with Kid Rena, Armstrong and others after arriving in New Orleans.
877.q: Yes. I tell you what, my mother, I'd go home with 30, 40 dollars and give my mother. And it would seem impossible for us to pick up that kind of money, a piece to go home with. And we have made good money. Made good money. Then I've had cousins and they would likewise. It wasn't three, it was six…

778.t: Playing billiard gardens for a dollar a night, tips and the kitty
778.s: Gardens served beer, crab boils; no union, a dollar a night plus tips; speakeasy and legality questions.

404.t: Safe streets in the 1930s and walking home from gigs
404.s: Harold and Mitchell contrast safe nights then with today, recalling walking home with a horn and cheap sandwiches.

404.q: and get a dine sandwiches and that. I mean.

So, we go in there and we, we play all night long. And when we get through, the guy gives us fifteen cents and a pack of…

841.t: Kingfish club, small combo and tips at the Famous Door
841.s: Harris recalls a four-piece combo with Smiling Joe, collecting tips, and generous gamblers at the Famous Door.

779.t: Happy Schilling, Johnny Lollard and Cadillac pay and tips
779.s: Clarifying Happy Schilling, Johnny Lollard as booster, and why Fishbaum and Buzzy Williams paid best, with tips at the Cadillac.
779.q: That's Happy, not his son. Oh, no, no, well, this is a long time ago. Yeah. And, yeah, I worked there. Yeah, he had, and then of course when Happy, a lot of times Happy Shillin used to get two jobs, and Johnny Lollard, Johnny was the fellow who played the jazz, the hornet, you know, and he also…

287.s: Parade pay was about three dollars top, advertising two dollars, and halls paid four or five dollars a band. The leader got a couple dollars more.
287.ch: Brass bands, funerals and working conditions
287.q: Oh it was cheap but you couldn't do so much with a dollar. You could go to the market and with a dollar and a half you couldn't carry the stuff away. We used to get highs, the player dads get three dollars, that was top money. Three dollars. Advertisement, there's about two dollars. And then the…

633.t: Private dance at Arnaud's and the ten-dollar pay
633.s: Questions about the private party job, hours and pay of ten dollars, and the layout of the place.
633.q: Not our band. No, I don't think. They're special. And at that dance, we was a play to one and the phone hired us an hour over. We was getting from ten to one. We sat at ten, play to one, that was, we was getting ten dollars for that job.

591.t: Saving money at the Tivoli and deciding to go to Europe
591.s: He describes the Tivoli job, pay versus tips, the Manti brothers, and reading about bands in Europe.
591.q: Yes. I was, I saved so much money. I was young. I didn't know what to do with it. And Frank and his brother, they made me save some, they taught me to save. And my mother was sick at the time. And I had to send my salary home and keep my tips. Was that good? The tips, the salary was nothing next to…

8.t: Pay in Chicago versus New Orleans
8.s: Chicago paid far better than the New Orleans district, where a night earned a dollar and a half plus tips; room rent was cheap in New Orleans.
8.q: Look, you play down the district. Now, all right. Go down there, you play from 9 o'clock, 4 o'clock in the month, of course, you make tips. You got only a dollar and a half of that.

571.s: Rockwell guesses sidemen earned about $26 a night and describes the length of sets and breaks.
571.ch: Rockwell: Los Angeles club and sessions

Well, that would have been... Tuesday and Wednesday... Well, somewhat more than scale, I guess. Or would that have been scale?…

681.t: Gulf Coast hotel and nightclub jobs and cheating waiters
681.s: Hirsch played Gulf Coast hotels for $17.50 a week plus food, and tells of two waiters who raised checks and robbed a slot machine.
681.ch: Gulf Coast and later working bands
681.q: Well, not in the 30s. Oh, in the 30s. No, it's when we were kids when we got used to, we'd get a job over there at the hotels. In the 30s, we'd get a job over at the hotels. 192.t: Young Tuxedo Band jobs, leader and pay

192.q: Well, Young Tuxedo Band used to play the New Orleans Country Club, Saturday nights, dinner dance, 8 to 12. 688.t: Advertising jobs, plentiful work then, and demanding his price
688.s: He describes playing in store advertising and athletic club jobs, how musicians used to be only musicians, and insisting on pay instead of food and drink.
688.q: Yes sir. And then I had a Petone's, uh, fighting arena, the fifth water athletic club. Every Friday. Where was that? That street? That athletic club on the domain between Decatur and Charlotte. And then I had a, uh, on the downtown side of the bank. Cause it was called the Fifth Water Athletic…

643.t: Where bands played, societies, pay and prices
643.s: Bands played in halls and parades for societies; pay was around twelve dollars for the band or less, and he recalls how far a dime or nickel went.
643.q: Oh no, they played in the hall. In the hall? That's how we used to play. We used to play all in the Orleans, I don't know, it took so long. We used to play parade. Play all over. Way back, way back to the country. We used to go down there and lick. And there's two-two boys way up the road there.…

51.t: Chicago clubs and freelance recording pay
51.s: The Entertainers on 35th, Ory's refusal to sign an exclusive contract, and earning up to $600 in a day freelancing.
51.q: Yeah, I made much of $600 one day. In Chicago? Yeah. When we were talking...

689.t: Lorenzo Tio, a New Orleans reading band, and Chicago pay

882.t: Tom Anderson's mouthpiece trick and tips
882.s: Correcting his pay at Anderson's to $25 and tips from actors; mention of a different Louis.

292.t: Hiring a colored band for $2 a man, c. 1930
292.s: A band hired for a nephew's 21st birthday cost two dollars a man; colored bands play jazz at carnival marching clubs.
292.q: That was 30 years ago. My daughter and my sister gave a party for my nephew. He was 21. He's 51 now. So that would be about 30 years ago. And my sister didn't remember the band. But I think it was six or an eight piece colored band. And it only cost $2 a man.

690.s: The band got about a dollar and a half for a parade and dance, later raised.
690.q: When I first started paying, we used to get, we'd average around a dollar and a half for a parade and the dance.

483.t: Pay, white and Black engagements, and Martin Behrman
483.s: Chris earned good gig pay plus tips, mostly played for white people but was known for funerals, and went on river trips with Martin Behrman.

780.t: Pay in the 1950s, five dollars for four hours
780.s: Gigs paid five or six dollars a piece; the whole band split five dollars after four hours.
780.ch: Touring, band and money in the 1950s-60s
780.q: You couldn't do anything like that, huh? Even for you? Sure. Everybody. Everybody got the same thing. Five or six dollars a piece. Even when you had the records out and everything? Things like the price should have gone up.

56.t: Band, crowd and pay at Pete Lala's
56.s: The band was four pieces, the crowd mixed, hours eight to four, pay $1.50 a night plus tips.

446.s: He left after eight months, married at 22, settled in Philadelphia; Chester paid 80 dollars a week.
446.q: Yes. But of course I mean I left the band in maybe about eight months then of course I mean I had gotten married, that’s right yeah. I got married at the age of 22 and there I just started the life of you know trying to get gigs and work and actually I did mostly musical shows in Philadelphia,…

122.t: Hampton's band in San Francisco; low road pay

He would do that, oh man he was a regular there. And the men loved to come to San Francisco because we had one of…

852.t: Salary with Maynard and selling CDs
852.s: The band paid a small salary with occasional raises; he opened shows and sold his first CDs for twenty dollars.
852.q: I had the connection to jazz you know. And I thought it was good work. And it didn’t pay that great so there were a lot of slightly more established musicians that wouldn’t do that gig.

824.t: Pay in the twenties and thirties compared

824.q: Now here we go. Back in 1923, with the Paul Whiteman Collegians, in 1923, six nights a week, I made a hundred bucks a week. And now wait. 984.t: Pay, rent and prices in the late 1950s
984.s: Five Spot pay, rent, prices and recording session fees around 1959-60.
984.q: At the Five Spot I made $90 per week, six nights a week. That was 1959. So I have to figure that’s like six or seven hundred dollars a week now. I could live easily off $90 a week at that time.

366.t: Pay at Jimmy Ryan's and specializing on clarinet
366.s: Sol earned $50 a week, never needed non-music jobs, and shows photographs with Rex Stewart.
366.q: Okay. I made $50 a week. And I was working I think it was six nights a week. And I’m talking about the 40s, Monk, 1946, ’47.

469.t: Joining Bobby Darin and the Ed Sullivan Show

469.q: So he said, “You’ve got to get a tux.” You know. I had to get a tux and the band, on The Ed Sullivan Show, it was Thad Jones in the trumpet section, his brother Hank Jones playing piano, they were all on staff, CBS staff man. 470.t: Busboy earnings and a bad tour with Mr. Hibbert

143.t: The Harlem club circuit and its pay

369.t: Orchestra Hall as a high point, Time magazine and the raise to $750
369.s: She outsold Horowitz, left Joe Sherman after a month, and Time's write-up lifted her pay from $250 to $750 a week.

328.s: Pay was terrible with the most popular leaders, while Dizzy paid well.
328.ch: Maynard Ferguson and Dizzy's big band
328.q: It was bad, unbelievably bad. The guys that were making the most money in most cases were paying the least. Lionel Hampton. He was the most popular band out there. Paid the least.

111.t: Tyree Glenn's Roundtable quartet and the hundred-dollar bills
111.s: He took Poppa Joe Jones's place in Tyree's group, played requests like 'Saints', and a customer laid $680 on his tom-tom.

452.s: Cobb remembers Fields as a warm roommate, is shocked when he reads of Fields's suicide in Miami, and recalls seeing Fields's $250 pay stub when he himself made $175.

453.t: Pay on the 1931 tour and Armstrong lending him money

233.t: Pay at $20 a night and the band as a family

566.q: $35. And eventually it went up to $50, and then it went up to $75. I think when I left I was making a $125, or something like that.
